events: Foundation Stone of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
title: Foundation stone of Sri Harmandir Sahib: Sai Mian Mir and the Golden Temple
desc: How the foundation of Sri Harmandir Sahib was laid in the sarovar at Amritsar in 1588, the part of Sai Mian Mir, and why the temple has four doors and sits low.
alt: Sri Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple, in the sarovar at Amritsar
body: This day remembers the laying of the foundation of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple, in the middle of the sarovar at Amritsar, at the end of the 1580s. The SGPC's calendar for Nanakshahi 558 lists the anniversary on two dates, one in summer and one at the start of the month of Magh, the date most often given by tradition.
## A temple in the pool

Sri Guru Ram Das Ji had founded the town of Ramdaspur and dug the sarovar, the pool of nectar that gave Amritsar its name. His son, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, completed the pool and resolved to build a house of the Guru in its centre. Tradition remembers that he invited his friend, the Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir of Lahore, to lay the foundation stone, a gesture of the respect the Gurus gave to people of every faith. Baba Budha Ji, Bhai Gurdas Ji and the sangat took part, and the building was completed in 1604, when the Adi Granth was installed in it.
## Built to be open

The Guru made choices that still speak. Sri Harmandir Sahib was set lower than the ground around it, so that every visitor walks down to it in humility. It was given four doors, one on each side, as a sign that it is open to people of every caste, creed and direction. The walkway across the water joins it to the Darshani Deori, the gateway.
## The temple through history

The temple was attacked and destroyed several times in the eighteenth century, and each time the Khalsa rebuilt it, the present building from 1764. In the early nineteenth century Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered its upper floors in gilded copper, which gave it the name the Golden Temple.
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather at Sri Harmandir Sahib for kirtan and Ardas, and many bathe in the sarovar.

events: Foundation Stone / Sirjana Divas – Sri Akal Takht Sahib
title: Sirjana Divas of Sri Akal Takht Sahib: the Throne of the Timeless
desc: In 1606 Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji built the Akal Bunga facing Sri Harmandir Sahib. The story of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, its role in the Panth, and how its Sirjana Divas is kept.
alt: Sri Akal Takht Sahib in a photograph of about 1870
cap: Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, about 1870
body: The Sirjana Divas of Sri Akal Takht Sahib remembers the founding in 1606 of the Throne of the Timeless, facing Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. It is the first and highest of the five Takhts, the seats of authority of the Sikh Panth.
## The Akal Bunga

After the shaheedi of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the young Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji built a raised platform across the courtyard from Sri Harmandir Sahib. Tradition remembers that Baba Budha Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji built it with their own hands, with no mason allowed to touch it but the Guru and his Sikhs. It was raised higher than the throne of any emperor, about twelve feet, a statement that the Sikhs answered to the Timeless One alone. It was called the Akal Bunga.
## Miri beside Piri

From the Akal Bunga the Guru held court, received the sangat, heard disputes and issued his commands, while Sri Harmandir Sahib remained the place of the Word and of kirtan. He watched wrestling and martial exercises in the courtyard, and in the evening ballads of heroism were sung there, the beginning of the dhadi tradition. The two buildings, facing each other, are a picture of Miri and Piri together.
## The voice of the Panth

In the eighteenth century the Sarbat Khalsa gathered at Sri Akal Takht Sahib to take decisions as the Guru Panth, and it remains the place from which hukamnamas to the whole Panth are issued. The building has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, most recently after June 1984.
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather for Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, and the Jathedar addresses the Panth.

events: Sampuranta Divas – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Sri Harmandir Sahib
title: Sampuranta Divas: the completion of the Adi Granth at Ramsar in 1604
desc: Sampuranta Divas remembers the completion of the Adi Granth by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji at Ramsar, Amritsar, in 1604, days before its first installation.
body: Sampuranta Divas remembers the completion in 1604 of the Adi Granth, the scripture that became Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Sampuranta means completeness. The day comes shortly before the Pehla Prakash Purab, when the finished Granth was installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib.
## Ramsar

To compile the Granth, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji withdrew to a quiet place outside Amritsar, beside a pool now called Ramsar, and worked there for about a year. Gurdwara Ramsar Sahib marks the place. The Guru gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, much of it from the pothis kept at Goindwal by the family of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, which Baba Mohan Ji, the third Guru's son, was persuaded to give. He added his own bani, and the compositions of fifteen Bhagats, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid, and of Bhatts and Sikhs of the Guru's court.
## Written by Bhai Gurdas Ji

The Guru dictated and Bhai Gurdas Ji, the learned Sikh who was also the Guru's maternal uncle, wrote it out. The bani was arranged with great care, by raag, the musical measure in which it is sung, and within each raag by author and form. At its head stands the Mool Mantar and Japji Sahib.
## Completion and installation

When the work was finished, it was carried in procession to Sri Harmandir Sahib and installed, with Baba Budha Ji as the first granthi. A century later, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji added the bani of the ninth Guru and gave the Granth the Guruship. Read about [the Pehla Prakash Purab](/gurpurab/pehla-prakash-purab-guru-granth-sahib-ji).
## How the day is observed
Sangats hold kirtan and Ardas at Sri Harmandir Sahib and Gurdwara Ramsar Sahib.

events: Marriage Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji & Mata Jito Ji (Guru Ka Lahore)
title: Marriage of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Mata Jito Ji at Guru Ka Lahore
name: Marriage Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji & Mata Jito Ji
desc: In 1677 Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji married Mata Jito Ji at a village near Anandpur Sahib that came to be called Guru Ka Lahore. The story and the Basant Panchmi mela.
body: This day remembers the marriage in 1677 of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Mata Jito Ji, at a place in the hills near Anandpur Sahib that has been known ever since as Guru Ka Lahore. It is celebrated on Basant Panchmi with a mela at Guru Ka Lahore, in the Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh.
## Why Guru Ka Lahore

Mata Jito Ji was the daughter of Bhai Hari Jas, a Sikh of Lahore. Her family wished the wedding to be held in Lahore with the Guru's procession coming to them. But the Guru, then a young man of about eleven, could not travel there in safety, since the Mughal authorities were hostile after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. So the Guru's family arranged for a small town to be laid out in the hills a few miles north of Anandpur Sahib, and named it Lahore, so that the bride's family could say the wedding had taken place at Lahore. It is remembered as Guru Ka Lahore, the Guru's Lahore.
## The springs of Guru Ka Lahore
Tradition remembers that there was no water at the place, and that the Guru struck the ground with his spear and his arrow, and springs came out that still flow, called Tir Ganga and Paatal Ganga.
## Mata Jito Ji

Mata Jito Ji was the mother of three of the Chaar Sahibzade: Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji. She lived at Anandpur Sahib, where she passed away in 1700, and Gurdwara Mata Jito Ji at Agampur, near Anandpur Sahib, keeps her memory.
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather at Gurdwara Guru Ka Lahore on Basant Panchmi for kirtan, Ardas and langar.

title: Basant Panchmi in Sikh history: Raag Basant, Chheharta Sahib and Guru Ka Lahore
desc: What Basant Panchmi means in the Sikh tradition: the season of Raag Basant at Sri Harmandir Sahib, the mela at Chheharta Sahib, and the Guru's marriage at Guru Ka Lahore.
body: Basant Panchmi, the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Magh, is the festival of spring across North India, when the fields of Punjab turn yellow with mustard flowers. In the Sikh tradition it is a day of several memories, and the SGPC's calendar keeps it as a day in Sikh history.
## Raag Basant

Raag Basant, the raag of spring, is one of the thirty-one raags of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, with bani by the Gurus and the Bhagats. The Gurus used the images of spring, of fresh growth and blossoming, to speak of the soul that blossoms when it remembers the Divine, rather than of outward festivity. At Sri Harmandir Sahib, by long tradition, kirtan in Raag Basant is sung through the season, beginning around Maghi and continuing until Hola Mohalla.
## Chheharta Sahib

At Chheharta, near Amritsar, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji had a large well dug for the villages around, worked by six Persian wheels, the chhe harte that gave the place its name. Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib marks the place, and a large mela is held there on Basant Panchmi, when sangats come for kirtan and to drink from the well.
## Guru Ka Lahore

Basant Panchmi is also the day on which Sikhs remember the marriage of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Mata Jito Ji at Guru Ka Lahore, near Anandpur Sahib, where a mela is held. Read about [the marriage at Guru Ka Lahore](/gurpurab/guru-gobind-singh-ji-mata-jito-ji-marriage-guru-ka-lahore).
## How the day is observed
Gurdwaras hold kirtan in Raag Basant, and many Sikhs wear yellow, the colour of the season and of the mustard fields.

events: Victory at Sirhind – Banda Singh Bahadur & Baba Deep Singh
title: Victory at Sirhind 1710: the battle of Chappar Chiri and the end of Wazir Khan
desc: On 12 May 1710 the Khalsa under Baba Banda Singh Bahadur defeated Wazir Khan at Chappar Chiri and took Sirhind, where the younger Sahibzade had been martyred. The story.
alt: The Fateh Burj tower at Chappar Chiri
cap: The Fateh Burj at Chappar Chiri, built in 2011 to remember the victory
body: This day remembers the battle of Chappar Chiri on 12 May 1710, in which the Khalsa led by Baba Banda Singh Bahadur defeated the army of Wazir Khan, the governor of Sirhind, and went on to take the city. For the Sikhs it was the answer to the martyrdom of the younger Sahibzade at Sirhind six years before.
## The road to Sirhind

Sent to Punjab by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1708, Banda Singh Bahadur gathered the Khalsa and took Samana, Sadhaura and other towns. Sikhs from across Punjab joined him, many from the Majha crossing the Sutlej to reach him. Wazir Khan, who had ordered the death of Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, raised a large army with artillery and elephants, and called for a holy war against the Sikhs.
## Chappar Chiri

The armies met on the plain of Chappar Chiri, about twenty kilometres from Sirhind. The Khalsa was outnumbered and lacked guns, and the early fighting went hard. Banda Singh Bahadur himself led a charge into the centre of the enemy line, and the Sikhs broke it. Wazir Khan was killed in the battle. Some accounts hold that Baba Deep Singh Ji fought there too, which is why the SGPC's calendar names both leaders. Two days later the Khalsa entered Sirhind.
## After the victory
Banda Singh Bahadur appointed a Sikh governor of Sirhind, set up his capital at Lohgarh and struck coins in the name of the Gurus. The Fateh Burj, the tower of victory, now stands at Chappar Chiri.
## How the day is observed
Sangats mark the day with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Chappar Chiri and Fatehgarh Sahib.

title: Chhota Ghallughara 1746: the lesser massacre in the marshes of Kahnuwan
desc: In 1746 the forces of Lahore under Lakhpat Rai trapped thousands of Sikhs in the marshes of Kahnuwan. About seven thousand were killed and three thousand executed in Lahore.
body: The Chhota Ghallughara, the lesser holocaust, was a massacre of Sikhs in the spring of 1746 in the marshy forests around Kahnuwan, near Gurdaspur, carried out by the forces of the Mughal administration of Lahore. Sikh sources say about seven thousand were killed in the fighting and three thousand more taken prisoner and executed in Lahore.
## Lakhpat Rai's revenge

In those years the Sikhs lived as fugitives in the forests and hills, with a price on their heads. In early 1746 a band of Sikhs killed Jaspat Rai, the faujdar of Eminabad, in a skirmish. His brother, Lakhpat Rai, a powerful minister at the court of Yahiya Khan, the governor of Lahore, swore to wipe out the Sikhs. He had Sikhs living in Lahore rounded up and executed, banned the reading of Gurmukhi, and ordered the destruction of Sikh places.
## The marshes of Kahnuwan

He then marched out with a large army, cannon and local levies. About fifteen thousand Sikhs, among them many families, took refuge in the swampy forests of Kahnuwan near the Ravi. The army surrounded the area and burned the forest. Trapped between the soldiers, the swamp, the river and the hills, where the hill rajas refused them shelter, the Sikhs fought their way out over several days, suffering terrible losses. The leaders who survived, among them Nawab Kapur Singh and Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, broke through and reached the Malwa.
## How it is remembered

The prisoners were taken to Lahore and executed at the Nakhas, where Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj stands. Within two years the Khalsa had regrouped into the Dal Khalsa. Sikhs remember the shaheeds with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, and at a memorial near Kahnuwan.

events: Leaving of Sri Anandpur Sahib Fort
title: Leaving Anandpur Sahib, December 1704: the siege and the broken oaths
desc: After a siege of months, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji left Anandpur Sahib on the night of 20 December 1704 on promises of safe passage that were broken within hours. The story.
cap: Anandpur Sahib, the town of the Khalsa
body: This day remembers the night in December 1704 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, his family and the Sikhs left the fort of Anandpur Sahib after a long siege. It begins the Shaheedi week of December, the most sorrowful days of the Sikh year, in which the Guru lost his mother and all four of his sons.
## The siege

The hill rajas had long resented the Guru's growing power and his Khalsa, which rejected caste and gave ordinary people dignity and arms. With the forces of the Mughal governors of Sirhind and Lahore, they besieged Anandpur Sahib through 1704. Food ran out; the Sikhs ate leaves and bark. Some Sikhs, worn down, signed a disclaimer saying they were no longer the Guru's Sikhs and left; they would return at Muktsar.
## The oaths

The besiegers sent promises of safe passage if the Guru would leave the fort. The rajas swore on the cow and the Mughal commanders on the Quran, and a letter was brought said to carry the emperor Aurangzeb's own oath. The Guru doubted them, and tradition remembers that he tested them by sending out bullocks loaded with rubbish, which the besiegers fell upon. In the end, at the pleading of the sangat and of his mother, Mata Gujri Ji, he agreed to go.
## The night of leaving

On the night of 20 December, in the cold and rain, the Guru, the Sahibzade, Mata Gujri Ji, Mata Sundari Ji, Mata Sahib Kaur Ji and the Sikhs left the fort. Within hours the oaths were broken and the army fell on them as they reached the Sirsa river. Read on: [the separation at the Sirsa river](/gurpurab/parivar-vichhora-sirsa-river).
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas, and many Sikhs begin the week of remembrance.

title: Parivar Vichhora: the separation of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji's family at the Sirsa
desc: On the night after leaving Anandpur Sahib in December 1704, the Guru's family was scattered at the flooded Sirsa river. What happened at Parivar Vichhora, and what followed.
alt: Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora on the Sirsa river
cap: Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora, on the bank of the Sirsa
body: Parivar Vichhora, the separation of the family, remembers what happened on the bank of the Sirsa river in December 1704, a few hours after Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji left Anandpur Sahib. In the dark and the flood, the Guru's family was scattered, and most of them never saw each other again.
## The attack at the river

The oaths of safe passage were broken almost at once. As the Guru's party reached the Sirsa, a stream swollen into a torrent by winter rain, the besieging armies attacked. Many Sikhs held back the attackers so that the others could cross, and many were swept away in the current. Precious manuscripts, among them much of the Guru's own writing, were lost in the water. Tradition remembers that the Guru held the morning Asa di Vaar kirtan on the bank even as the battle went on.
## Three ways

In the confusion the family was split into three. The Guru, his two elder sons, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, and about forty Singhs crossed and rode towards Chamkaur. Mata Gujri Ji and the two youngest, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, were carried downstream and taken in by their former cook, Gangu, who betrayed them at Sirhind. Mata Sundari Ji and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji were escorted to Delhi by Bhai Mani Singh Ji. Within a week the elder sons fell at Chamkaur and the younger were martyred at Sirhind.
## How the day is observed

Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora stands on the bank of the Sirsa, near Ropar, and sangats gather there for kirtan and Ardas. Read on: [the Saka of Chamkaur Sahib](/gurpurab/saka-chamkaur-sahib) and [the Saka of Sirhind](/gurpurab/saka-sirhind-chhote-sahibzade-mata-gujri-ji).

title: Darbar Khalsa on Dussehra: what the day means in the Sikh calendar
desc: Why the SGPC's calendar marks Dussehra as Darbar Khalsa: the Khalsa's gatherings, the shastar tradition at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, and the Sikh view of the festival.
body: The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar marks Dussehra as Darbar Khalsa, a day when the Khalsa gathers in darbar. While Dussehra is a Hindu festival celebrating the victory of Rama over Ravana, in the Sikh tradition the day is kept in its own way, as a gathering of the Khalsa and an occasion to honour the shastar, the weapons that the Gurus gave the Khalsa to defend the weak.
## The Khalsa in darbar

In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa lived as fugitives and fought for survival, its bands came together at set times of the year to meet, to take decisions as the Sarbat Khalsa and to plan. Vaisakhi and Diwali at Amritsar were the best known of these gatherings. Festival days, when people were on the move in any case, allowed the scattered jathas to meet. A darbar of the Khalsa on such a day is a reminder of a community that governed itself in the presence of the Guru.
## The tradition at Hazur Sahib

At Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji spent his last days, Dussehra is kept with a great procession in which the Takht's historic weapons are carried out and displayed, and the Nihang Singhs and sangat take part. Many Nihang Singh dals hold their own gatherings and displays of gatka on the day.
## A Sikh reading of the day
The Gurus taught that victory over evil begins with victory over the five thieves within: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Katha on the day often turns to this inner meaning.
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas, and in some places the shastar are honoured.

title: Morcha Guru Ka Bagh 1922: the non-violent struggle that shook the Raj
desc: In 1922 Sikh jathas went day after day to cut firewood at Guru Ka Bagh, near Amritsar, and were beaten by police without striking back. The story of the morcha.
body: The Morcha Guru Ka Bagh was a non-violent campaign in 1922 at Gurdwara Guru Ka Bagh, about twenty kilometres from Amritsar, during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. For weeks, jathas of Sikhs walked to the gurdwara and were beaten by the police without lifting a hand in return, and their courage moved people across India and abroad.
## Firewood for the langar

Guru Ka Bagh, at the village of Ghukewali, is associated with visits by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. Like many shrines, it had been in the hands of a mahant, who had agreed to hand it to the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. But when Sikhs cut firewood for the langar from the trees on the gurdwara's land, as they always had, the mahant complained of theft, and in August 1922 the police arrested five Sikhs.
## Jatha after jatha

The SGPC began sending jathas each day to cut wood, each member pledged to non-violence. At the bridge near the gurdwara the police beat them with lathis until they fell, day after day. Hundreds were injured and thousands arrested. The Rev. C. F. Andrews, a friend of Gandhi, came to watch and wrote that he had seen a new heroism, and that the Sikhs had learned the lesson of the cross. Even a jatha of retired soldiers, many decorated in the First World War, took the blows.
## The outcome

Under public pressure, the beatings stopped in September, and in November the land was bought by a sympathiser and handed over. The morcha strengthened the movement that led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.
## How the day is observed
Sangats remember it with kirtan and Ardas at Guru Ka Bagh and elsewhere.

title: Chabiyan Da Morcha: the keys of the Toshakhana and the first victory
desc: In 1921 the British seized the keys of the Toshakhana of Sri Harmandir Sahib. The Sikhs' non-violent Morcha of the Keys won them back on 19 January 1922. The story.
alt: The square in front of Sri Akal Takht Sahib in about 1924
cap: The square in front of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, about 1924
body: Chabiyan Da Morcha, the Morcha of the Keys, was a non-violent campaign in 1921 and 1922 to recover the keys of the Toshakhana, the treasury of Sri Harmandir Sahib, from the British authorities. Its success on 19 January 1922 was the first great victory of the Gurdwara Reform Movement.
## The keys

Under British rule, the management of Sri Harmandir Sahib was in the hands of a manager, the sarbrah, appointed by the government. In 1920 the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee was formed to bring the gurdwaras under the Panth's own care, and in October 1921 it asked the sarbrah to hand over the keys of the Toshakhana, which holds the shrine's treasures. Instead, the Deputy Commissioner of Amritsar sent an official to collect the keys from him.
## The morcha

The SGPC declared that the Sikhs would not accept government control of their gurdwara. Meetings were held across Punjab, and Sikhs began wearing black turbans in protest and refusing to cooperate. Many leaders, among them Baba Kharak Singh, the president of the SGPC, were arrested, and hundreds of Sikhs courted arrest. The movement stayed non-violent throughout.
## The keys returned

Faced with mass protest, the government released the prisoners and, on 19 January 1922, sent an official to hand the keys to Baba Kharak Singh at a large gathering at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won.
## How the day is observed
Sangats remember it with Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib and with katha about the reform movement.

title: Jaito Da Morcha: the Akhand Paath at Gangsar and the firing at Tibbi Sahib
desc: In 1923 an Akhand Paath at Gurdwara Gangsar, Jaito, was broken off by the authorities. The morcha that followed, the firing on the shaheedi jatha in February 1924, and the mela.
cap: Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib, Jaito, where the morcha began
body: Jaito Da Morcha was a long non-violent campaign of 1923 to 1925 at Jaito, in today's Faridkot district, during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. It is remembered each year with a mela at Jaito, on the anniversary of the firing on the shaheedi jatha in February 1924.
## The interrupted Akhand Paath

In 1923 the British forced Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha, who sympathised with the Akali movement, to give up his throne. Sikhs gathered at Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib in Jaito, a town then in Nabha state, to hold an Akhand Paath and pray for his restoration. In September 1923 the police arrested the sangat and broke off the reading before it was complete. For Sikhs, interrupting an Akhand Paath was an intolerable insult to the Guru.
## The jathas

The SGPC began sending jathas to Jaito to complete the Akhand Paath. Each was arrested. On 21 February 1924, a shaheedi jatha of five hundred Sikhs, followed by thousands of sympathisers, reached Gurdwara Tibbi Sahib near Jaito. The state forces opened fire. Many were killed and many more wounded. The jathas kept coming, from Punjab and from Sikh communities as far away as Canada and Shanghai.
## The outcome

The morcha ended in 1925 with the passing of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act. The authorities allowed the Akhand Paath to be completed at Gangsar, and in August 1925 one hundred and one Akhand Paaths were held there together.
## How the day is observed
A mela is held at Jaito on the anniversary, with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas at Gurdwara Gangsar Sahib and Gurdwara Tibbi Sahib.

events: Sardar Baghel Singh – conquest of Delhi (fixed solar anniversary)
title: Sardar Baghel Singh and the Khalsa in Delhi, 1783: the gurdwaras of Delhi
name: Sardar Baghel Singh – conquest of Delhi
desc: In March 1783 Sardar Baghel Singh led the Khalsa into Delhi and stayed to build seven gurdwaras at the places of the Gurus, among them Sis Ganj, Rakab Ganj and Bangla Sahib.
alt: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk around 1915
cap: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, Delhi, about 1915, first built by Sardar Baghel Singh in 1783
body: This day remembers March 1783, when the Khalsa under Sardar Baghel Singh entered Delhi and raised the Nishan Sahib over the Red Fort. The SGPC's calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date. Its lasting legacy is the gurdwaras of Delhi, which Baghel Singh built at the places linked to the Gurus.
## Sardar Baghel Singh

Baghel Singh was born in the 1730s near Amritsar and rose to lead the Karorsinghia Misl, with lands in the Doaba and around Chhalaudi. In the 1770s and 1780s the misls made repeated expeditions across the Yamuna into the lands around Delhi, where the Mughal empire had grown weak.
## Into Delhi

In March 1783 Baghel Singh, with Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, led a large Khalsa force into Delhi. Their camp outside the city, where thirty thousand horsemen were gathered, is remembered in the name of the area Tis Hazari. The Khalsa entered the Red Fort, and the emperor Shah Alam II came to terms with them.
## The gurdwaras of Delhi

Baghel Singh agreed to withdraw most of his men on condition that he could stay with a small force to find and mark the places linked to the Gurus, and receive part of the city's revenue to build them. With the help of local people, he identified seven places, and built gurdwaras at them: Mata Sundari Ji, Bangla Sahib, Rakab Ganj, Sis Ganj, Moti Bagh, Majnu Ka Tilla and Bala Sahib. Many of Delhi's best-known gurdwaras stand on his foundations.
## How the day is observed
Delhi's sangat celebrates the day as Fateh Divas with kirtan, Ardas and Nagar Kirtan.
